# Introduction

## What is a README?

-   A text file that sits with your data or code and explains what it is, how it
    was made and how to use it. It is usually called `README.md` or
    `README.txt` and kept in the top folder.

-   Often the first thing a person sees and sometimes the only documentation they
    read. Sites such as GitHub display it on the front page of a project.

-   Without one, data and code cannot be easily interpreted, reproduced or
    credited. 

-   Formal metadata standards are generally preferable where one fits your data.
    A README is the practical option where there is no suitable standard, and the
    quickest way to document your work for yourself and your collaborators.

## Best practices

These are adapted from guidance by Cornell Data Services[^1].

-   Write one README for each logical group of files, such as a dataset made of
    several similar files or a set of related scripts

-   Name it so that it is clearly linked to the files it describes (if it sits within a top level of a repository then naming it README is acceptable)

-   Use plain text (txt or Markdown is fine) rather than a Word or Google doc

-   Separate pieces of
    information with blank lines instead of one long paragraph

-   If you write several READMEs, use the same order and the same terms in each

-   Write dates as YYYY-MM-DD (ISO 8601)

-   Use standard names and vocabularies for taxa, places and other keywords

[^1]: Cornell Data Services, [Writing READMEs for Research
    Data](https://data.research.cornell.edu/data-management/sharing/readme/) and
    [Writing READMEs for Research Code &
    Software](https://data.research.cornell.edu/data-management/sharing/writing-readmes-for-research-code-software/).
    Both are licensed under CC BY 4.0.

# Exercises

## What to include

Use a **data README** when your project mainly processes data using software, and
a **code README** when the software itself is the main product. Many projects
need parts of both.

The tables show the minimum content that Cornell recommends for reuse.

### README for data

| Section | Minimum content |
|:--------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------|
| General information | Dataset title, who collected the data and how to contact them, date(s) of collection, where it was collected |
| Data and file overview | Each file name with a short description, and when each file was created |
| Sharing and access information | The licence or any restrictions on use |
| Methodological information | How the data were collected or generated, how they were processed from the raw data, and any software or instruments needed to interpret them, with version numbers |
| Data-specific information | Every variable with its full name and definition, the units, and the codes used for missing data |

Also worth including: keywords, funders, how to cite the data, links to
publications that use it, quality-assurance steps, and definitions of any
quality flags.

### README for code

| Section | Minimum content |
|:--------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------|
| General information | Project name, version number and a one sentence description |
| Project overview | A fuller description, the date of creation or latest release, what is where (code, tests, configuration, dependencies, documentation) and the total size |
| Installation | Step-by-step set-up, system requirements, dependencies with versions, anything to configure by hand and known issues |
| Usage | How to run it and what output to expect, and known limitations |
| Licence | The licence and how to cite the code |
| Contact information | The principal investigator and the maintainer |
| Acknowledgements | Funders and grant numbers |

Cornell also offers a downloadable template for each, which you can adapt:
[data README template](https://hdl.handle.net/1813/116815.2) and
[code README template](https://hdl.handle.net/1813/116816.3).

## Exercise 1: Strong and weak READMEs

Here are two READMEs for the same fictional dataset: a study of how quickly oak
and ash leaves rot in woodland.

### A weak README

``` markdown
# Litter data

Data for my thesis. Collected 2022-2023.

Files: bags.csv, bags2_final.csv

Columns are explained in the paper. Ask me if you have questions.
```

### A stronger README

``` markdown
# Leaf litter decomposition in lowland woodland, 2022-2023

## General information

- **Authors:** A. Example and B. Sample, University of Life
- **Contact:** litter-data@example.org
- **Collected:** 2022-10-12 to 2023-10-14 at six woodland plots
- **Funding:** Example Trust, grant 12345

## Data and file overview

`litterbag_mass.csv` - One row per litter bag per collection date (created 2024-01-20)
`plot_description.csv` - One row per plot, with canopy cover and location

## Sharing and access information

- **Licence:** CC BY 4.0
- **Cite as:** Example, A. and Sample, B. (2024). Leaf litter decomposition
  data. University of Anywhere Data Repository.

## Methodological information

Dried leaves (10 g) were sealed into 5 mm mesh bags and placed in each plot in
October 2022. One bag per species per plot was collected after 90, 180, 270
and 365 days, then re-dried and weighed on a 0.01 g balance.

## Data-specific information: `litterbag_mass.csv`

48 rows and 6 variables.

| Variable | Description | Units |
|:---------|:------------|:------|
| `plot` | Plot identifier | P1 to P6 |
| `species` | Leaf species | `OAK` or `ASH` |
| `days` | Days in the field | days |
| `mass_init_g` | Dry mass at the start | g |
| `mass_final_g` | Dry mass at collection | g |
| `notes` | Comments, for example why a bag is missing | text |

Missing values are blank. They are bags that were lost or torn open.
```

🎬 In your group, compare the two READMEs

🎬 Use the tables above to work out what each one includes and what is missing

🎬 List the five most important problems with the weak README


## Exercise 2: Draft a README from a case study

### Scenario

You are a research assistant in an ecology group. A colleague has just finished a
field season and is about to leave on fieldwork again. She has handed you a folder
and asked you to write a README for it so that other people can use it. She has
written down what she can remember.

### The folder

``` text
pond-survey/
├── data/
│   ├── raw/pond_survey_2024.csv
│   └── clean/pond_survey_2024_clean.csv
├── scripts/
│   ├── 01_clean_data.R
│   └── 02_summarise.R
├── outputs/
│   ├── fig1_richness_by_pond.png
│   └── model_summary.txt
└── pond-survey.Rproj
```

### The colleague's notes

These are exactly as she wrote them. They are informal, and they are not
complete.

-   Pond invertebrate survey, 2024. I wanted to know if cattle access to ponds
    affects the number of invertebrate families.

-   Two sites. MR = Marsh Reach, fenced off from cattle since 2019. HF = Heath
    Farm, which is grazed. Three ponds at each (MR1 to MR3 and HF1 to HF3).

-   I visited each pond once a month from May to August (`visit` 1 to 4). At each
    visit I took a 3 minute sweep sample with a pond net (1 mm mesh) and identified
    everything to family in the lab. `tn` is the number of families and `ab` is the
    total number of individuals.

-   I measured the water at each visit with a handheld probe, 10 cm below the
    surface: `temp` is water temperature, `ph` is pH and `do` is dissolved oxygen.

-   If a reading failed I typed -999. `flag` says what happened: 0 is fine, 1 is a
    problem with the probe and 2 is where the pond was partly dry and I cut the
    sweep short.

-   `01_clean_data.R` changes the -999s to NA and writes the clean file.
    `02_summarise.R` makes the figure and fits a mixed model of family richness with
    site as the main effect and pond as a random effect, leaving out the flag 2
    rows.

-   I used R 4.3.1 with tidyverse 2.0.0, here 1.0.1 and lme4 1.1-35. Open the
    project file in RStudio, then run script 01 and then 02.

-   Funded by a small grants scheme from the university. I will have to find the
    grant number.

-   I have not decided on a licence yet. Maybe CC BY? Not sure whose email address
    to put as the contact. Probably my supervisor's.

### Your task

🎬 In your group, draft a README for the `pond-survey` folder, using the tables
above to decide what to include. Choose someone to write and let everyone
contribute

🎬 The folder has both data and code, so your README will need parts of both

🎬 Write `[to be confirmed]` where information is missing. A README that shows its
gaps is better than one that hides them or guesses

🎬 Keep a list of the questions you would need to ask the colleague

::: {.callout-important title="Challenge"}
Which of the missing items would cause the most trouble for someone trying to use
the data?
:::

## Live demonstration: a README for code

We will look at a code repository, find what is missing from its README and
improve it live. Use the code README table above to follow along.

### repo contents

```text
woodland-birds/
├── data/
│   └── bird_counts.csv
├── scripts/
│   ├── 01_summarise_counts.R
│   └── 02_plot_counts.R
├── outputs/
│   ├── species_totals.csv
│   └── fig_species_totals.png
├── LICENSE
├── README.md
└── woodland-birds.Rproj
```
### the README

``` markdown
# woodland-birds

**Version:** 1.0.0

R scripts that total the birds counted for each species in a woodland point-count survey and plot the results.

## Project overview

The scripts read a small table of bird counts (site, date, species and count), add up the counts for each species and draw a bar chart of the totals. The example data are a short extract from a larger survey.

**Date of latest release:** 2024-06-30

**What is where:**

- `data/bird_counts.csv`: the bird counts (input data)
- `scripts/`: the R code, numbered in the order to run it
- `outputs/`: the results made by the scripts (a table and a figure)
- Configuration files: none (the `.Rproj` file only sets the working folder)
- Dependencies: listed under Installation
- Documentation: this README

**Total size:** about 15 KB

## Installation

**System requirements:** Windows, macOS or Linux. RStudio is recommended. Some basic packages are required.

**Steps:**

1. Install R and RStudio.
2. Download this folder and unzip it.
3. Open R and install the required packages

**Known issues:** species names must contain no spaces, use underscores instead.

## Usage

1. Open `woodland-birds.Rproj` in RStudio.
2. Open `scripts/01_summarise_counts.R` and click **Source**.
3. Open `scripts/02_plot_counts.R` and click **Source**.

Run the scripts in this order, because the second one uses the output of the first.

**Expected output:**

- `outputs/species_totals.csv`: total count for each species, largest first
- `outputs/fig_species_totals.png`: bar chart of the totals

**Limitations:** the counts are raw totals and are not adjusted for survey effort.

## Licence

Code is released under the MIT licence (see `LICENSE`).

**Cite as:** Example, A. (2024). *woodland-birds* (Version 1.0.0) [Computer software]. University of Anywhere.

## Contact information

- **Principal investigator:** Dr B. Sample, University of Life (b.sample@example.org)
- **Maintainer:** A. Example, University of Life (a.example@example.org)

## Acknowledgements

Funded by the Example Trust, grant number 12345.
```

::: {.callout-important title="Challenge"}
Could you install and run the code using only the README? Which items from the
Installation and Usage rows are missing?
:::

## Discussion: your own projects

This part of the workshop is optional.

🎬 Think of a dataset or a piece of code of your own

🎬 Which three items from the checklist would you struggle to include today?

🎬 What is the one thing you could add that would help someone most?

If you would like feedback on a README of your own, you can share it with a
neighbour or the group.

# Summary

-   A README explains your data or code to people who were not there when it was
    made, so that it can be understood, reproduced, reused and credited.

-   Cornell recommends five sections for data (general information, data and file
    overview, sharing and access, methods, and data-specific information) and
    seven for code (general information, project overview, installation, usage,
    licence, contact and acknowledgements).

-   Strong READMEs define every variable and its units, explain missing-value
    codes, give software versions, list the steps in order and include a licence,
    a citation and a contact.

-   Check for sensitive data and anything you have been asked not to disclose.

-   It is fine to show gaps. A README that says "to be confirmed" is better than
    one that guesses.

-   Start from a template and ask a colleague to test your README.
